title: The Rabshakeh at the Wall
sum: Hezekiah son of Ahaz becomes king of Judah and is praised as no other king of Judah: he removes the high places, smashes the standing stones and even breaks up the bronze snake of Moses, which people had been burning incense to. He trusts the LORD, rebels against Assyria and defeats the Philistines. The narrator then looks back to the fall of Samaria in Hezekiah's sixth year, and says why it fell: Israel would not listen.

In Hezekiah's fourteenth year Sennacherib seizes the walled towns of Judah. Hezekiah apologizes, pays a huge tribute and strips the temple doors. Even so, three Assyrian officers arrive at Jerusalem's water channel with an army, and the Rabshakeh gives a speech in Hebrew, over the heads of Hezekiah's ministers, to the men on the wall. Whom do you trust? Egypt is a broken reed; Hezekiah has torn down the LORD's own altars; no god has ever saved a land from Assyria. The people say nothing, as the king ordered.
readings: Read as history

Much of the chapter can be checked. Sennacherib's own annals describe the 701 BC campaign against Hezekiah, the capture of 46 walled towns, and a tribute of gold and silver; the reliefs from his palace at Nineveh show the siege of Lachish. Many historians accept 18:13–16 as drawn from an archival record, and see the Rabshakeh's speech as a plausible picture of Assyrian psychological warfare, which their own letters describe.
Read as composed speech

The speech is also a piece of theology placed in an enemy's mouth. Its questions about trust (the Hebrew root batach comes eight times in 18:19–30) are the questions the whole book of Kings asks. The Rabshakeh's claim that the LORD sent him (18:25) is what Isaiah himself said of Assyria (Isaiah 10:5–6), and his scorn for Hezekiah's reform turns a mark of loyalty into a charge of impiety.
Read as two accounts

Critical scholars since Bernhard Stade usually divide 18:13–19:37 into an annal-like account A (18:13–16), which ends in tribute and says nothing of a miracle, and two prophetic accounts, B1 (18:17 to the first half of 19:9, with 19:36–37) and B2 (the rest of 19:9 to 19:35). On this view the chapter brings together the bitter memory of surrender and a later faith that Zion was saved.

views.H: A faithful king, a real invasion and a real speech at the wall. Hezekiah's payment in 18:14–16 shows his fear before he learned to trust; the speech that follows tests whether Judah will trust the LORD or Egypt.
views.C: The praise of Hezekiah (18:3–7) is the Deuteronomistic writer's ideal, matched only by Josiah (23:25). The account of Samaria's fall (18:9–12) repeats 17:5–6. Account A agrees closely with the Assyrian annals; the Rabshakeh's speech belongs to account B1, perhaps written down in Josiah's time or later.
views.A: Sennacherib's annals (the Taylor and Chicago prisms and the Jerusalem prism) list Hezekiah's tribute as 30 talents of gold and 800 of silver, with his daughters, musicians and furnishings. The Lachish reliefs show the city's capture. Nimrud letters show Assyrian officers arguing with a city's people in their own tongue, as the Rabshakeh does.
views.J: The rabbis praised Hezekiah for hiding a book of cures and for breaking the bronze snake (Mishnah Pesahim 4:9; Bavli Berakhot 10b). One Talmudic tradition says the Rabshakeh was a renegade Israelite, which would explain his fluent Hebrew (Bavli Sanhedrin 60a).
views.X: Christian readers have taken the Rabshakeh's question, "What is this trust?", as the question of faith itself. The breaking of Nehushtan, which Jesus compares to his own lifting up (John 3:14), is read as a warning that even a God-given symbol can become an idol.

deep.h: Did Hezekiah pay, and how much?
deep.b: Kings says Hezekiah paid 300 talents of silver and 30 of gold (18:14). Sennacherib's annals say 30 talents of gold and 800 of silver, along with precious stones, ivory couches, his daughters and musicians, sent after the Assyrian king went home to Nineveh. The gold agrees exactly. The silver may differ because the Assyrian figure counts everything taken, or because the scales differed, or because Assyrian scribes inflated their totals. Either way, the two sources agree on the main fact the narrator does not hide: Hezekiah surrendered and paid. Kings places the payment before the speeches; Sennacherib's annals place it after the campaign. Many historians think Kings' account A has moved the payment to the start, so that the story of rescue can follow.

deep.h: Why does the Rabshakeh speak Hebrew?
deep.b: Aramaic was already the language of diplomats (18:26), and Hezekiah's ministers want the talks kept from the soldiers on the wall. The Rabshakeh refuses, because his real audience is the common soldier who will starve. A letter from Nimrud records Assyrian officials talking to the people of Babylon at the city gate, asking them to give up their rebel leaders; this was a known tactic. A rabbinic tradition explains his good Hebrew by making him an apostate Jew (Bavli Sanhedrin 60a); modern scholars note that many Assyrian officials were from the West and spoke its languages.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the speech answers the reform
deep.b: The Rabshakeh's most surprising argument is that Hezekiah has offended the LORD by removing his high places and altars (18:22). This may be more than clever propaganda: it may reflect what many Judeans really thought. Closing the country shrines in a time of crisis would have looked like impiety to villagers who had worshipped the LORD at them for centuries, and the fall of 46 towns would have seemed like proof. If so, the narrator lets the enemy voice a real local objection to centralized worship, so that the rescue of Jerusalem in chapter 19 can answer it. The core idea, that the Rabshakeh voices a real local objection to the reform, is common in the commentaries. What Claude adds is the suggestion that the narrator places it here on purpose, so that chapter 19 can answer it. That part is speculation; nothing outside the text confirms that such an objection was raised.

echoes: Numbers 21:8–9; John 3:14; 2 Kings 17:5–6; Isaiah 36:1–22; 2 Chronicles 32:1–19; Isaiah 30:1–7; Isaiah 31:1–3; Ezekiel 29:6–7; Micah 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:8

settings.what: Hezekiah's submission
settings.by: Hezekiah king of Judah
settings.to: Sennacherib king of Assyria, at Lachish
settings.when: After Sennacherib took the walled towns of Judah in 701 BC
settings.why: 'I have done wrong... Whatever you lay on me, I will carry.' A vassal's surrender, paid for with the Temple's gold. Kings tells it plainly before the great rescue story, so readers see that even a king who trusted the LORD first tried to buy peace. Sennacherib's own annals record the tribute.

settings.what: The Rabshakeh's first speech
settings.by: The Rabshakeh, chief officer of Sennacherib
settings.to: Hezekiah, through his officials Eliakim, Shebna and Joah, at the water channel of the Upper Pool
settings.why: Assyrian propaganda meant to break Jerusalem's will. It asks 'What is this trust of yours?' and attacks each support in turn. Egypt is a crushed reed. The LORD is offended by Hezekiah's removal of the high places. The LORD himself sent Assyria. The speech raises the question the whole story answers. For readers in exile, who had seen Babylon win, it asked whether trust in the LORD is foolish when empires are strong.
views: Many historians: Assyrian officers did address besieged cities, and the speech fits Assyrian arguments, so it may preserve a real event.
Childs and others see two accounts woven together (18:17–19:9a and 19:9b–35), each shaped to make a theological point. On this view the first account (B1) is 18:17–19:9a with its ending in 19:36–37.

settings.what: The officials' request and the Rabshakeh's refusal
settings.by: Eliakim, Shebna and Joah; then the Rabshakeh
settings.to: The Rabshakeh; then Hezekiah's officials
settings.why: The officials ask him to speak Aramaic, the language of diplomats, so the people will not understand. He refuses and says his message is for the men on the wall, who will eat their own dung in the siege. The exchange shows that Assyria's real target was the ordinary people, and it turns the speech into an open bid for their loyalty.

settings.what: The Rabshakeh's speech to the men on the wall
settings.by: The Rabshakeh, shouting in Judean
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem sitting on the wall
settings.why: To split the people from their king. He tells them not to let Hezekiah fool them. He offers them peace and a new land 'of grain and new wine' if they surrender, and mocks the gods of Hamath, Arpad and Samaria. The offer of deportation to a good land sounds like a parody of the LORD's own promises. The people's silence, by Hezekiah's order, is the right answer. For exiles who had been deported, the speech named their temptation: to think the LORD was one more failed god.

traditions.q: Hezekiah smashed the bronze snake Moses had made, because the people burned incense to it (2 Kings 18:4). Should churches have images?
views: Yes. The Second Council of Nicaea (787) taught that icons are to be honored with a bow and a kiss, while worship belongs to God alone, and that the honor passes to the one the icon shows. Hezekiah destroyed the snake because it had been worshiped as a god, which an icon must never be.

Yes, on the same teaching: to venerate an image is not to adore it, and the honor goes to the person it shows (Catechism 2129–2132). Since God became visible in Christ, Christ and the saints may be pictured.

Images may stay if they are not worshiped. Luther opposed those who smashed images (Against the Heavenly Prophets, 1525), so Lutheran churches kept crucifixes and paintings; what is wrong is trusting in an image, not the image itself.

No images in worship. The Heidelberg Catechism says God must not be pictured, and that his people are to be taught by the living preaching of his word, not by images (Q&A 96–98). Reformers who cleared the churches of Zurich and Scotland often pointed to Hezekiah and Josiah.

title: The Night of the Angel
sum: Hezekiah tears his clothes, goes into the temple and sends to Isaiah. The prophet answers that the Assyrian king will hear a report, go home, and die by the sword there. Sennacherib, hearing that Tirhakah of Cush is marching against him, sends a letter instead: no god has saved any land from Assyria. Hezekiah spreads the letter out before the LORD and prays that all the kingdoms of earth will know that the LORD alone is God.

Isaiah sends back a long poem. Daughter Zion laughs at the boastful king; God planned his conquests long ago and will lead him home with a hook in his nose. A sign is given: two years of self-sown grain, then sowing and harvest again. That night the angel of the LORD strikes the Assyrian camp, and 185,000 lie dead in the morning. Sennacherib goes home to Nineveh, and years later his own sons kill him while he worships his god.
readings: Read as miracle

The angel's blow is God's direct act, like the death of Egypt's firstborn (Exodus 12:23). Traditional Jewish and Christian readers have taken it this way, and the Assyrian records never claim Jerusalem was taken. Sennacherib boasts that he shut Hezekiah up "like a bird in a cage," a way of describing a siege that did not end in capture.
Read as history behind the story

Many historians think a real event lies behind it: a plague in the camp, which Herodotus's story of mice gnawing the Assyrian bowstrings (Histories 2.141) may also remember; or the threat from Egypt and Cush; or a negotiated withdrawal after tribute. The numbers are large and may have grown.
Read as theology

Critical scholars often see account B2 (the second half of 19:9 to 19:35) as a later theological story that grew around the memory that Jerusalem was not taken in 701. Its point is the claim of Hezekiah's prayer: the LORD alone is God, and the gods of Assyria's victims were wood and stone.

views.H: Isaiah's word comes true on every point: Sennacherib hears a report, withdraws, never shoots an arrow at Jerusalem, and dies by the sword in his own land. The angel's work is a real act of God, though how it was done is not described.
views.C: Account B1 (19:1 to the first half of 19:9, with 19:36–37) and account B2 (the rest of 19:9 to 19:35) tell the story twice, with a prophetic word, a threat and a deliverance in each. The murder of Sennacherib happened in 681 BC, twenty years later; the story presses the events together. The poem in 19:21–28 may be older material from Isaiah.
views.A: Sennacherib's annals boast of taking 46 walled towns and of shutting Hezekiah in Jerusalem, but claim no capture of the city, and the tribute comes to Nineveh afterward. The Babylonian Chronicle records his murder by "his son" in a revolt; Esarhaddon's inscriptions blame his brothers. A letter to Esarhaddon names the murderer, read by Simo Parpola as Arda-Mulissi, who may be the "Adrammelech" of 19:37.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition, sung in the Haggadah poem "Va-amartem zevach Pesach" ("And you shall say, it is the Passover sacrifice"), places the blow on Passover night, and the Talmud says the Assyrians' souls were burned while their bodies were left whole (Bavli Sanhedrin 94a). It also says God wanted to make Hezekiah the Messiah but did not, because he sang no song after his rescue (Bavli Sanhedrin 94a).
views.X: The church fathers read the destruction of Sennacherib's army as a sign that God protects his people, and the rescue is read in the liturgy alongside Christ's victory. Lord Byron's poem "The Destruction of Sennacherib" (1815) made it one of the best-known scenes in English literature.

deep.h: The Prism, Lachish and the angel: three ways to put them together
deep.b:
We have unusual evidence for this campaign: Sennacherib's annals (on the Taylor, Chicago and Jerusalem prisms), the Lachish reliefs from his palace, the destruction layer at Lachish itself (Level III), and the biblical accounts in Kings, Isaiah and Chronicles. All agree that Assyria devastated Judah and that Jerusalem was not taken. They differ on why.

A miracle. Many readers take 19:35 at its word. They note that the Assyrian annals never record a defeat, so the silence is what we would expect, and that the tribute coming after the king's return fits a withdrawal Sennacherib could not explain. A natural cause. Others suggest disease in the camp, pointing to Herodotus's report from Egyptian priests that mice ate the bowstrings and quivers of Sennacherib's army at Pelusium (Histories 2.141), since mice are linked with plague in 1 Samuel 6:4–5. The location and details do not match Kings, so the link is uncertain. Theology over memory. Most critical scholars think Hezekiah's surrender and payment (18:14–16) is the history, and the angel story is a later faith that the LORD defends Zion, which grew strong in Josiah's day and failed in 586.

Two campaigns. A harmonizing view, argued by John Bright, keeps both the surrender and the rescue as history by placing them in two campaigns, 701 and about 688 BC, with Tirhakah's title as one argument (see below). No Assyrian record supports a second campaign, and most historians now reject it.

The text itself does not choose a mechanism. It says only that the angel of the LORD struck, and that Sennacherib went home.

Tirhakah (Taharqa) was a Cushite (Nubian) king of Egypt's 25th dynasty. He became pharaoh in 690 BC, eleven years after 701, so some take "king" in 19:9 as the title he held when the story was written, and others think he led the army as a young prince under his brother Shebitku. Assyrian records mention an Egyptian and Cushite army defeated at Eltekeh in 701. For those who argue for a second campaign around 688, Tirhakah's title is a main reason.

echoes: Isaiah 37:1–38; 2 Chronicles 32:20–23; Exodus 12:23; Isaiah 10:5–19; Isaiah 31:8; Psalm 46; Psalm 48; Psalm 76; Deuteronomy 4:28; 1 Samuel 17:26; Nahum 1:11–13

settings.what: Hezekiah's message to Isaiah
settings.by: Hezekiah, through Eliakim, Shebna and the elders of the priests in sackcloth
settings.to: Isaiah son of Amoz
settings.why: 'The children have come right to the mouth of the womb, but there is no strength to push them out.' Hezekiah admits Judah's helplessness and asks the prophet to pray for 'the remnant still here.' The message shows a king who turns to the LORD's prophet, not to Egypt. Exiles could take it as words for their own helplessness.

settings.what: Isaiah's first oracle
settings.by: Isaiah, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Hezekiah's servants, for their master
settings.why: 'Don't be afraid.' The LORD will put a spirit in the king of Assyria; a report will send him home, and he will die by the sword. The oracle answers the Rabshakeh's insults as insults against the LORD. Its fulfillment is told at the end of the chapter (19:36–37).

settings.what: Sennacherib's letter
settings.by: Sennacherib king of Assyria, through messengers
settings.to: Hezekiah king of Judah
settings.when: When news came that Tirhakah of Cush was marching out
settings.why: To keep the pressure on while the army turned away: 'Don't let your God... fool you.' The letter now attacks the LORD himself, not just Hezekiah. That sharpens the test for readers: the question is no longer whether Hezekiah can resist, but whether the LORD is like the gods of the nations.

settings.what: Hezekiah's prayer
settings.by: Hezekiah
settings.to: The LORD, 'seated on the cherubim,' with the letter spread out before him in the Temple
settings.why: The prayer confesses that the LORD alone is God over every kingdom. It admits that Assyria really did destroy the nations' gods, because they were only wood and stone. Then it asks for rescue. 'Then every kingdom on earth will know that you, LORD, are God, and only you.' The prayer turns a political crisis into a question of God's name among the nations. For exiles it was a model of how to pray under an empire, and it echoes Solomon's prayer in the same house (1 Kings 8:41–43).

settings.what: Isaiah's answer: the taunt song, the sign and the oracle
settings.by: Isaiah son of Amoz, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Hezekiah; the taunt song is addressed to Sennacherib, and the sign to Judah's survivors
settings.when: In answer to Hezekiah's prayer, during the crisis of 701 BC
settings.why: Three parts. The taunt (19:21–28) has Daughter Zion laugh at the boastful king. The LORD says he planned Assyria's conquests long ago and will lead the king home with a hook in his nose. The sign (19:29–31) promises that a remnant will take root again. The oracle (19:32–34) promises the city will not be attacked, 'for David my servant's sake.' For the first hearers it was rescue; for exiles it was a promise that a remnant from Zion would grow again.
views: Traditional and many critical readers: the core comes from Isaiah himself; the same text stands in Isaiah 37.
Childs, Clements and others: parts, such as the remnant sign, were added later, perhaps in Josiah's day or the exile, to apply the rescue to new readers.

title: Fifteen More Years
sum: Hezekiah falls sick and Isaiah tells him he will die. Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and weeps, and before Isaiah has left the palace courtyard God sends him back: "I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears." Hezekiah will live fifteen more years, and Jerusalem will be shielded. A fig poultice is laid on the sore, and as a sign the shadow on the steps of Ahaz goes back ten steps.

Then envoys arrive from Merodach-baladan of Babylon, and Hezekiah shows them everything in his treasuries. Isaiah announces that all of it, and some of Hezekiah's own sons, will be carried off to Babylon. Hezekiah calls the word good, and wonders aloud whether there will at least be peace in his own days. The chapter closes with a mention of his water channel.
readings: Read as history

The illness, the envoys and the tunnel all fit Hezekiah's later years, though the order is debated: if the envoys came in 703, when Merodach-baladan briefly ruled Babylon again, the illness came before the invasion of 701, and the link to the 14th year (18:13) is a schematic count; some place the envoys in his first reign, 721–710. Merodach-baladan was a Chaldean king of Babylon who fought Assyria for decades and looked for allies in the West. The 15 added years agree with Hezekiah's 29-year reign if he fell sick in his 14th year (18:2).
Read as prophetic legend

The sign of the shadow, the healing prayer and the oracle against Babylon belong to stories about Isaiah told among his followers. Many scholars think the oracle of 20:17–18 was shaped after 597 or 586, when Judah's treasures and princes really were taken to Babylon (24:13–15).
Read as turning point

The chapter turns the story's eyes from Assyria to Babylon. The king who trusted God in chapter 19 is praised for his prayer and faulted for his pride, and his calm answer in 20:19 leaves readers to judge him.

views.H: The sign was a real miracle, a reversal of the shadow on a stair that served as a sundial; Hezekiah's display of his wealth was a real lapse into pride, and Isaiah's warning was fulfilled a century later.
views.C: The story is told out of order: the envoys most likely came before 701, when Hezekiah still had treasures to show (18:15–16). The editor placed chapter 20 after the rescue so that the story of Babylon would lead on to the exile.
views.A: Assyrian inscriptions describe Merodach-baladan (Marduk-apla-iddina II) ruling Babylon in 721–710 and again briefly in 703. The Siloam inscription, cut in the tunnel that brought the Gihon spring's water into the city, describes the moment the two teams of diggers met. Fig poultices appear in Ugaritic texts for treating horses.
views.J: The Talmud says Hezekiah's illness came because he would not marry and have children, and that Isaiah told him he would lose both this world and the world to come; Hezekiah answered that he had a tradition from his ancestors that one keeps praying even with a sword at one's throat (Bavli Berakhot 10a). The rabbis listed the "hiding of the book of cures" among his praised acts (Mishnah Pesahim 4:9).
views.X: Hezekiah's prayer and tears have been read as a model of prayer that changes God's announced plan, and his song in Isaiah 38 was sung in the church's morning office as a canticle. Some Christian readers fault his answer in 20:19 as selfish; others read it as humble acceptance.

deep.b: Verse 20 mentions only in passing that Hezekiah "made the pool and the channel and brought the water into the city"; 2 Chronicles 32:30 adds that he blocked the upper outlet of the Gihon spring and brought the water down to the west side of the City of David. In 1880 a boy found an inscription in the tunnel that still carries the Gihon's water 533 meters (about 1,750 feet) to the Pool of Siloam. It tells how the diggers, working from both ends, heard each other's voices and broke through "pick against pick." Most scholars date the tunnel and the inscription to Hezekiah's reign on the evidence of the script; a 2003 study of radiocarbon in plant matter and uranium-thorium in stalactites supported a date around 700 BC. The date is still debated. Ronny Reich and Eli Shukron, from their excavations of the spring's older water systems and the pottery, argued that the tunnel was cut earlier, around 800 BC; others reply that the radiometric dates and 2 Chronicles 32:30 point to Hezekiah. John Rogerson and Philip Davies argued for a much later, Hasmonean date, a view few have followed. Hezekiah's date is the majority view, not a settled one. The tunnel's winding path is still debated: following a natural crack in the rock is the most common explanation.

The "steps" (Hebrew ma'alot) can mean the steps of a staircase or the marks of a dial. Ahaz may have built an outdoor stair on which a shadow crept down as the sun moved; the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) at Isaiah 38:8 reads "the steps of the upper room of Ahaz," which would put the stair at a roof room like the one in 23:12. Readers have explained the shadow's return as a miracle in the heavens, a local miracle of light, or an eclipse; the text says only that the LORD turned the shadow back.

echoes: Isaiah 38:1–22; Isaiah 39:1–8; 2 Chronicles 32:24–33; Psalm 6:6; Joshua 10:12–14; 2 Kings 24:13–15; 2 Kings 25:13–17; Daniel 1:3–4

settings.what: Isaiah's sentence, Hezekiah's prayer and the reversal
settings.by: Isaiah for the LORD; Hezekiah; then the LORD again through Isaiah
settings.to: Hezekiah on his sickbed; the LORD; then 'Hezekiah, ruler of my people'
settings.when: In Hezekiah's illness, around the time of the Assyrian crisis
settings.why: The LORD announces death, Hezekiah prays with tears, and before Isaiah has left the courtyard the LORD adds fifteen years and promises to shield the city. The scene shows that a sentence spoken by a prophet can be changed by prayer. For exiles under a sentence of judgment, it was a reason to pray.

settings.what: The sign of the shadow
settings.by: Hezekiah and Isaiah; Isaiah cries to the LORD
settings.to: Each other; then the LORD
settings.why: Hezekiah asks for a sign, chooses the harder one, and the shadow goes back on the steps of Ahaz. The sign confirms the promise of healing. It also contrasts Hezekiah with his father Ahaz, who refused a sign (Isaiah 7:10–12).

settings.what: Isaiah's oracle of the Babylonian exile
settings.by: Isaiah, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: Hezekiah, after he showed his treasures to the envoys of Merodach-baladan
settings.when: Probably about 703 BC, when Babylon was seeking allies against Assyria
settings.why: Everything in the palace, and some of Hezekiah's sons, will be carried to Babylon. Hezekiah's reply, 'Is it not good, if there will be peace... in my days?', is either humble acceptance or selfish relief. This is the first mention of Babylon as Judah's fate. For exiles in Babylon it showed that their captivity had been foretold more than a century before.
views: Some readers: Hezekiah bows to God's word and gives thanks for mercy in his time.
Others: his answer shows a king thinking only of himself, a sign of the pride Chronicles mentions (2 Chronicles 32:25).

title: The Worst King
sum: Hezekiah's son Manasseh reigns fifty-five years, the longest reign in Judah's history, and undoes everything his father did. He rebuilds the high places, sets up altars for Baal and the army of the heavens inside the temple courts, places a carved image of Asherah in the house where God put his name, burns his son, and consults omens and spirits. Worse, he leads Judah to do more evil than the nations driven out before Israel.

God speaks through unnamed prophets: Jerusalem will be measured with the line used on Samaria and wiped out like a bowl turned upside down. Manasseh also fills Jerusalem with innocent blood. His son Amon follows his father's road for two years until his own servants kill him; the people of the land kill the plotters and crown eight-year-old Josiah.
readings: Read as history

Assyrian records confirm that Manasseh was a loyal vassal: Esarhaddon lists "Manasseh king of Judah" among the kings who sent building materials to Nineveh, and Ashurbanipal lists him among those who helped his campaign to Egypt. His long reign was a time of peace and recovery under Assyria.
Read as the sin that sealed Judah's fate

For the writer of Kings, Manasseh is the reason for the exile (23:26; 24:3–4). This chapter gathers every sin Deuteronomy forbids, almost in the order of Deuteronomy 18:10–11, and makes Manasseh worse than Ahab and the Amorites.
Read beside Chronicles

2 Chronicles 33 tells that Manasseh was taken in chains to Babylon, prayed, was restored and removed his idols. Kings says nothing of this. Readers have weighed the two accounts very differently: see the deep section below.

views.H: Manasseh's long rule, his worship of the heavens and his child sacrifice are recorded as fact; the unnamed prophets' sentence on Jerusalem stands, as later chapters show (24:3–4).
views.C: The list of sins is built from Deuteronomistic language and is partly a mirror of Josiah's reform in chapter 23. Some scholars think the editor made Manasseh the scapegoat for a disaster that otherwise seemed unexplained after Josiah's piety. Many date 21:10–15 to the exile.
views.A: Esarhaddon's Nineveh prism and Ashurbanipal's Cylinder C name Manasseh (Menasi) of Judah as a tributary king. Seals and figurines from 7th-century Judah, including many small pillar-figurines, show a mix of household religion that many think fits this chapter's picture of worship.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition holds that Manasseh had Isaiah killed, sawn in two while hidden in a cedar (Bavli Yevamot 49b), and debates whether he has a share in the world to come; the Mishnah lists him among kings who do not, but the rabbis say he was received because he repented (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2; Bavli Sanhedrin 101b–103a).
views.X: The "Prayer of Manasseh," a short penitential psalm, was included in many Greek and Latin Bibles and in the Apocrypha of the KJV. Christians have held Manasseh up as proof that no sinner is beyond God's mercy. Hebrews 11:37's "sawn in two" is often linked with the tradition of Isaiah's death.

deep.h: Manasseh: blamed in Kings, forgiven in Chronicles
deep.b:
Kings blames Manasseh for the fall of Judah three times (21:11–15; 23:26; 24:3–4) and records no repentance. 2 Chronicles 33:10–17 says the commanders of Assyria's king took him to Babylon with hooks and bronze chains; there he humbled himself, prayed, and was brought back to Jerusalem, where he took the foreign gods out of the temple and rebuilt the LORD's altar.

Readers explain this difference in several ways. Both are true. Kings tells only what decided Judah's fate; Chronicles adds what Kings left out. An Assyrian king might well have called a vassal to account, and Assyria reasserted control over Babylon in 648 BC. Chronicles reshapes. Many critical scholars think the Chronicler, who believed each generation is punished for its own sins, needed a reason for Manasseh's 55-year reign and found it in a repentance he inferred or built. Kings reshapes. Others think Kings made Manasseh blacker than he was, because the writer needed a cause for 586 after praising Josiah so highly. Whatever the history, the two portraits ask different questions: Kings, why did judgment fall? Chronicles, can a sinner come back? This site sets out both and does not choose between them.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a bowl turned upside down
deep.b: The picture of 21:13, wiping a bowl and turning it on its face, may have more in it than "emptying." A bowl was turned over after a meal was finished and cleaned. If that is the image, the city is not smashed like a pot (as in Jeremiah 19:10–11) but wiped and put away, which fits the exile: Jerusalem is emptied but not destroyed for ever. Commentators usually take the image as total emptying. Claude knows of no published form of this softer reading, though it may exist; it is a possible reading of the image, not one the chapter makes explicit.

echoes: Deuteronomy 18:9–14; 2 Chronicles 33:1–25; Jeremiah 15:4; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 19:3–6; 1 Samuel 3:11; Amos 7:7–9; Hebrews 11:37

settings.what: The LORD's promise for the Temple, quoted
settings.by: The LORD, as quoted by the narrator
settings.to: David and Solomon, recalled for the readers of Kings
settings.when: Quoted to show what Manasseh's idol violated
settings.why: The promise that the LORD would put his name in this house for all time, and would never again send Israel wandering if they kept Moses' law. Kings sets it beside Manasseh's idol to show that the condition had been broken. Exiles read it knowing the 'if' had been fatal.

settings.what: The prophets' sentence on Jerusalem
settings.by: The LORD, through his unnamed servants the prophets
settings.to: Manasseh king of Judah and the people of Judah and Jerusalem
settings.when: During Manasseh's long reign, about 687–642 BC
settings.why: Jerusalem will be measured with Samaria's line and wiped out like a bowl turned upside down. The oracle makes Manasseh's sins the reason for the coming exile. For exiles it was the clearest answer to 'why?': the judgment was announced in advance and Judah had been warned, as Israel was. Chronicles, writing later, tells the same reign with Manasseh's repentance (2 Chronicles 33:10–13).
views: Cross and many others: the blame on Manasseh comes from the exilic edition, explaining why even Josiah's reform could not save Judah.

Traditional readers: real prophets of Manasseh's day spoke this warning. Jewish tradition names prophets of his reign such as Joel, Nahum and Habakkuk (Seder Olam), and Isaiah, whom Manasseh was said to have killed (Bavli Yevamot 49b).

title: The Scroll in the Temple
sum: Josiah becomes king at eight and walks in David's road without swerving. In his eighteenth year he sends Shaphan the secretary to the temple to arrange payment for repairs. There Hilkiah the high priest hands Shaphan a scroll he has found: "the scroll of the law." Shaphan reads it to the king, and Josiah tears his clothes.

The king sends a delegation to Huldah, a woman prophet living in Jerusalem. Her answer has two parts. Everything in the scroll will fall on Jerusalem, because its people have abandoned the LORD for other gods. But because Josiah's heart was soft and he humbled himself, he will be gathered to his grave in peace and will not see the disaster.
readings: Read as history
Traditional readers take the scroll to be the law of Moses, lost or hidden during Manasseh's long reign and found again during repairs. Its threats of curse and exile would explain Josiah's alarm.
Read as the birth of Deuteronomy

Since W. M. L. de Wette (1805), most critical scholars have identified the scroll with an early form of Deuteronomy. Many think it was written not long before, by priests or scribes, and "found" to give the reform authority; others think it was an older northern collection brought south after 722.
Read as a story about hearing

However the scroll came to be, the story shows a king who responds to what he hears. Josiah weeps, seeks the LORD, and calls a woman prophet to explain the word. The book of Kings makes him the model of what every king should have been (Deuteronomy 17:18–20).

views.H: Hilkiah found a real, ancient scroll of the law of Moses, probably Deuteronomy or the whole Torah, which had been neglected under Manasseh and Amon. Huldah's word came true: Josiah died before the exile.
views.C: The scroll was some form of Deuteronomy, probably chapters 12–26 with 28, newly written or newly revised. The account itself was written by the same school that wrote Deuteronomy, and the finding may be a pious fiction. Huldah's promise of a peaceful death (22:20) did not come true in the plain sense, which suggests her words were not invented after the fact.
views.A: Kings in the ancient Near East often claimed to have found old foundation texts while repairing temples, as Nabonidus of Babylon did. Bullae (clay seal impressions) from the City of David bear the name "Gemaryahu son of Shaphan," which many link with Shaphan's family (Jeremiah 36:10).
views.J: The Talmud says Josiah, reading the threat of Deuteronomy 28:36 that the king would go into exile, hid the ark (Bavli Yoma 52b); medieval commentators add that the scroll was found rolled open at that verse. The rabbis also ask why Josiah sent to Huldah rather than to Jeremiah: because women are more tender-hearted, and she would pray for mercy (Bavli Megillah 14b).
views.X: Christian readers see in Josiah's response the right response to Scripture: hearing, grief and obedience. Jerome and other church fathers identified the scroll with Deuteronomy, long before modern critics. Huldah is remembered among the prophetic women of the Bible.

deep.h: What was the scroll? The debate
deep.b: The text calls it "the scroll of the law" (22:8) and "the covenant scroll" (23:2), and its contents can be inferred: it threatened curses on disobedience (22:13, 22:16–19), required one place of worship (23:8–9) and a Passover kept "as written" (23:21), and forbade mediums and spirits (23:24). All of these are distinctive of Deuteronomy, and nearly all scholars, traditional and critical, agree that the scroll was some form of it. They disagree on its age. Mosaic and rediscovered: the scroll was the law of Moses (or the Torah), lost during Manasseh's reign; its finding during repairs is natural, since documents were kept in temples (Deuteronomy 31:26). Older northern law: the scroll was a collection of northern traditions, perhaps from Levites or prophets, brought to Jerusalem after 722 and laid up in the temple. Recent composition: following de Wette and Wellhausen, the scroll was written in the late 7th century to support Josiah's reform, and the story of its finding gave it ancient authority. Some recent scholars go further and think the whole story of the finding was written later. The site follows no single view; the notes on 22:8 and 23:2–3 give the evidence.

Huldah is one of only a few women in the Hebrew Bible called a prophet, with Miriam, Deborah and Noadiah. Her husband kept the wardrobe, either the king's or the temple's. That the king's men went to her, though Jeremiah and Zephaniah were active at the time, shows she was a recognized prophet. Rabbinic tradition named the southern gates of the temple mount the Huldah Gates (Mishnah Middot 1:3); her tomb has been placed on the Mount of Olives since the Middle Ages.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a widening circle of hearing
deep.b: The scroll is read three times, each time to a larger audience: Shaphan reads it to himself (22:8), then to the king (22:10), and the king reads it to all the people, small and great (23:2). That the scroll is read in stages is often noted in the commentaries. Claude suggests a further point: the pattern acts out Deuteronomy's own rule that the law be read aloud before all Israel, men, women, children and foreigners (Deuteronomy 31:9–13), and so the story shows the scroll doing what it says it must do. Claude knows of no published form of this link, though it may exist; it is a suggestion, not something the text states.

echoes: Deuteronomy 17:18–20; Deuteronomy 28:15–68; Deuteronomy 29:27; Deuteronomy 31:24–26; 2 Chronicles 34:1–28; 1 Kings 13:2; Jeremiah 36:10–12; Jeremiah 26:24

settings.what: Josiah's orders for the Temple repairs
settings.by: King Josiah
settings.to: Shaphan the secretary, for Hilkiah the high priest
settings.why: Orders that follow the method of Jehoash (12:9–15): count the silver gathered at the door and pay the workers, who need not keep accounts because they work in good faith. The orders set the scene for the finding of the scroll. For readers they show the reform beginning with care for the LORD's house.

settings.what: Josiah's charge to seek the LORD
settings.by: King Josiah
settings.to: Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan and Asaiah
settings.when: After hearing the scroll of the law read
settings.why: 'Go and seek the LORD for me, for the people and for all Judah.' The king admits that the ancestors had not obeyed the scroll and that the LORD's anger has caught fire. It is a model of a leader taking the law to heart. Readers who knew the ending would feel the weight of a king who listened too late for his people.

settings.what: Huldah's oracle
settings.by: Huldah the prophet, speaking for the LORD, the God of Israel
settings.to: Josiah's officials, with one word for 'the man who sent you' and another for 'the king of Judah'
settings.why: Two answers. Disaster will fall on Jerusalem, as the scroll says, because the people left the LORD. But Josiah, who humbled himself, will be gathered to his grave in peace and not see it. The oracle confirms the scroll as the LORD's word and shows that a humble king can be spared, even when the nation is not. For exiles it explained why the best of kings could not stop the end.
views: Many readers: 'in peace' means before the disaster, and Josiah did die before Jerusalem fell, though in battle (23:29–30).
Some critical scholars think the promise was spoken before Josiah's violent death and left as it was, a sign that it is genuine.
Readers note that the king's officials go to Huldah, not to Jeremiah or Zephaniah, and the text shows no surprise. The Talmud discusses why (Bavli Megillah 14b).

traditions.q: The king's officials went to the prophet Huldah for God's word (2 Kings 22:14). Does her example open church leadership to women?
views: Huldah shows that God gives women the gift of prophecy, and the Church honors women such as Catherine of Siena and Teresa of Ávila as Doctors of the Church. But it teaches that it has no authority to ordain women as priests, since Christ chose only men as apostles (John Paul II, Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994; Catechism 1577).

Many Pentecostals see Huldah, Deborah and Philip's daughters (Acts 21:9) as proof that the Spirit calls women to speak for God. The Assemblies of God has given women ministry credentials since 1914 and opened the office of pastor to them in 1935. Its position paper Women in Ministerial Leadership (2025), which follows an earlier paper of 1990, names Huldah among its examples.

Wesley at first doubted, then allowed some women to preach when he saw an extraordinary call. American Methodists have given women full clergy rights since 1956, and most Methodist churches now ordain women.

Baptists are divided. The Baptist Faith and Message limits the office of pastor to men (article 6), and its supporters say Huldah was a prophet, not a pastor or elder. Other Baptist bodies, such as American Baptist Churches USA, ordain women.

Reformed churches are divided too: the Presbyterian Church in America ordains only men, while the northern church that is now part of the Presbyterian Church (USA) began ordaining women as ministers in 1956. Calvin treated women leaders such as Deborah as an extraordinary act of God that did not change the ordinary rule.

title: Josiah's Reform
sum: Josiah gathers the people, reads them the whole scroll, and makes a covenant before the LORD. Then he purges Judah. He removes the objects made for Baal, Asherah and the army of the heavens from the temple; dismisses the idol priests; burns the Asherah pole; tears down the shrine-men's rooms; defiles the high places from Geba to Beersheba and the child-sacrifice site of Topheth; removes the horses and chariots of the sun; and pulls down the altars of Ahaz and Manasseh and the shrines Solomon built for foreign gods.

He goes north to Bethel, burns bones on Jeroboam's altar as a man of God had foretold three centuries before, and spares that prophet's grave. He holds a Passover such as had not been held since the judges. No king before or after was like him. Yet the LORD's anger over Manasseh does not turn. Josiah is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Neco, and the last kings begin: Jehoahaz, taken to Egypt after three months, and Jehoiakim, set up by Neco.
readings: Read as history

Most historians accept that Josiah carried out a religious reform in the 620s, as Assyria's grip loosened, and that it included centralizing worship in Jerusalem. Archaeology has been debated: some sanctuaries, like the one at Arad, seem to have been closed in this period or earlier, and the drop in certain images after Josiah's time is noted, though evidence is mixed.
Read as idealized reform

Many critical scholars think the account is written to make Josiah the perfect king of Deuteronomy, undoing every sin listed in Kings in turn, from Solomon's shrines to Jeroboam's altar to Manasseh's altars. Some doubt that the reform reached Bethel and Samaria, then Assyrian provinces.
Read as tragedy

The greatest king dies suddenly in battle, and the next sentence is that the anger did not turn (23:26). Readers in every age have asked why reform did not save Judah. Chronicles answers that Josiah would not listen to Neco's warning (2 Chronicles 35:21–22); Kings gives no reason.

views.H: Josiah's reform was real, thorough and costly; the fulfilment of the 1 Kings 13 prophecy by name shows God's word governs history. His death was God's mercy, as Huldah said: he did not see the fall.
views.C: The reform account has been edited in stages: an original list of reforms, later expanded with polemic against Bethel and Samaria. The phrase "Josiah by name" in 1 Kings 13:2 is widely taken as an addition made after the fact. Many date the first edition of Kings to Josiah's reign, ending in praise of him, with a second edition after 586 adding 23:26–25:30.
views.A: The Babylonian Chronicle records that in 609 an Egyptian army came to help Assyria at Harran, which fits 23:29 ("toward the king of Assyria"). Herodotus says Neco defeated the "Syrians" at Magdolos (Histories 2.159), perhaps Megiddo. The Mesad Hashavyahu ostracon and the Arad letters come from this period.
views.J: Josiah is praised in Ben Sira 49:1–3 as sweet as honey. The Talmud says Josiah hid the ark and the anointing oil before the exile (Bavli Yoma 52b; Bavli Horayot 12a). The mourning for Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:25) is linked by some to Zechariah 12:11's mourning at Megiddo.
views.X: Matthew's genealogy includes Josiah (Matthew 1:10–11). Christian readers have often seen Josiah as a model reformer, and Protestant reformers appealed to him when removing images. His death raises the question of suffering righteous rulers that Christian readers link to the cross.

deep.h: Josiah's reform and Deuteronomy, point by point
deep.b: Almost every act in 23:4–24 matches a law in Deuteronomy. One place of worship: the closing of the high places (2 Kings 23:8) and Deuteronomy 12:13–14. The army of the heavens: the removal of the sun's horses and the star-priests (2 Kings 23:5, 23:11) and Deuteronomy 4:19 and 17:3. Asherah poles and standing stones: 2 Kings 23:6, 23:14 and Deuteronomy 7:5 and 12:3. Shrine men: 2 Kings 23:7 and Deuteronomy 23:17. Child sacrifice: Topheth (2 Kings 23:10) and Deuteronomy 12:31 and 18:10. Mediums and spirits: 2 Kings 23:24 and Deuteronomy 18:11. The country priests: Deuteronomy 18:6–8 lets them serve in the central sanctuary; 2 Kings 23:9 says they did not, which many see as a sign that the reform did not follow the scroll in every detail. Passover at the chosen place: 2 Kings 23:21–23 and Deuteronomy 16:1–8. And the summary of 2 Kings 23:25, with heart, being and strength, echoes the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:5).

deep.h: Why did Josiah die at Megiddo?
deep.b: Kings says only that Neco met Josiah and killed him (23:29). It does not say there was a battle. Chronicles tells of a battle, a warning from Neco that God had sent him, and archers who wounded Josiah (2 Chronicles 35:20–24); 1 Esdras 1:25–31 follows Chronicles. Historians have suggested that Josiah went to Megiddo as a vassal to meet the new pharaoh, and was executed for some suspected disloyalty, or that he tried to block Egypt's road to Assyria. The Babylonian Chronicle shows that Egypt was marching to help Assyria in 609, which explains why Neco was in a hurry. For the narrator, Josiah's early death fulfils Huldah's promise that he would not see the disaster (22:20), but readers have long felt the tension with the promise that he would go to his grave "in peace."

deep.title: Claude's theory: the bones and the Passover
deep.b: The reform reaches its climax with bones: Josiah fills the places of the poles with human bones (23:14), burns bones on the Bethel altar (23:16) and on the altars of Samaria (23:20), and spares only the bones of the prophet (23:18). Then comes the Passover (23:21). In Numbers 9:6–12 contact with a corpse makes a person unfit to keep Passover. Placing the Passover straight after a campaign that defiles every rival shrine with corpse impurity may be deliberate: the rivals are made unclean for ever, while Jerusalem, alone, is fit for the feast. This links two parts of the chapter that usually are read apart. Commentators often note that the bones defile the rival shrines for ever; Claude knows of no published link between this and the Passover rule of Numbers 9, though it may exist. It is a suggestion; the text does not draw the connection.

echoes: 1 Kings 13:1–3; 1 Kings 11:5–7; Deuteronomy 12:1–14; Deuteronomy 16:1–8; Deuteronomy 6:5; 2 Chronicles 34:29–35:27; Jeremiah 22:10–19; Zechariah 12:11; Ben Sira 49:1–3

settings.what: The reading of the covenant scroll and the covenant
settings.by: King Josiah
settings.to: All the men of Judah and Jerusalem, the priests, the prophets and all the people, small and great, in the LORD's house
settings.why: The king reads the whole scroll aloud and makes a covenant before the LORD to keep its commands with all heart and being. The people take their stand in it. The scene is a national renewal like Moses' at Moab (Deuteronomy 29) and Joshua's at Shechem (Joshua 24). It binds every Judean, not just the king, to the law. For readers it is the high point of Kings, and a model for renewal after exile (Nehemiah 8–10).
views: Since de Wette, most scholars: the scroll was a form of Deuteronomy, perhaps written or edited shortly before.
Traditional readers: a copy of Moses' law, perhaps the one kept by the ark (Deuteronomy 31:26), lost during Manasseh's reign.

settings.what: Josiah at the grave of the man of God
settings.by: King Josiah and the townspeople of Bethel
settings.to: Each other, at the altar of Bethel
settings.why: The townspeople identify the grave of the man of God from Judah who foretold this very day (1 Kings 13:2), and Josiah orders his bones left in peace. The exchange closes a prophecy given three centuries before. Readers see that the LORD's word waits for its time and comes true.

settings.what: Josiah's order to keep the Passover
settings.by: King Josiah
settings.to: All the people of Judah
settings.why: 'Hold a Passover for the LORD your God, by what is written in this covenant scroll.' The order brings the feast to Jerusalem as one national celebration, as Deuteronomy 16:1–8 commands, not a feast in each home. Kings says nothing like it had been held since the judges. For readers it was a picture of a whole people united around the one place the LORD chose.

settings.what: The LORD's word against Judah
settings.by: The LORD, as reported by the narrator
settings.to: Spoken about Judah; reported to the readers of Kings
settings.when: After Josiah's reform, looking ahead to the end
settings.why: Even after the best of kings, the LORD did not turn from his anger over Manasseh. He says he will put Judah away as he did Israel and throw off Jerusalem and the house. The word tells readers that the exile was not a failure of the reform but a sentence already passed. It is meant to quiet the question of why Josiah's goodness did not save them.

title: Babylon Comes
sum: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon defeats Egypt and makes Jehoiakim his vassal. After three years Jehoiakim rebels, and God sends raiding bands against Judah, because of Manasseh's sins and the innocent blood he shed. Jehoiakim dies and his son Jehoiachin reigns three months.

Babylon's army besieges Jerusalem, Nebuchadnezzar comes himself, and Jehoiachin surrenders with his mother and court. The king of Babylon carries off the temple and palace treasures and takes into exile the king, the leaders, the soldiers and the skilled craftsmen, leaving only the poorest. He sets up Jehoiachin's uncle Mattaniah as king and renames him Zedekiah. Zedekiah does evil, and rebels against Babylon.
readings: Read as history

The Babylonian Chronicle confirms this chapter in remarkable detail: in his seventh year Nebuchadnezzar marched to the land of Hatti, besieged "the city of Judah," and on the second of Adar (March 16, 597 BC) seized the city, captured the king, appointed a king of his own choice, and took heavy tribute to Babylon.
Read as judgment

The narrator explains the raids as the LORD's doing (24:2–4) and the treasures' removal as fulfilment of Isaiah's word (20:17). The exile of 597 is the first act of the end that Manasseh's sins made certain.
Read as the start of two communities

The deportation of 597 divided Judah. The exiles in Babylon, with Jehoiachin and Ezekiel, and those who stayed with Zedekiah each came to see themselves as the true remnant (Jeremiah 24; Ezekiel 11:14–17).

views.H: Each step of the fall is told as history and as God's judgment. The number of exiles differs within the chapter (10,000 in 24:14, 7,000 plus 1,000 in 24:16), which some explain as two counts of different groups.
views.C: The theological framework (24:2–4, 24:20) is from the exilic edition of Kings. The two lists of exiles in 24:14 and 24:15–16 are often taken as two sources. Jeremiah 52:28 gives a much smaller figure, 3,023, perhaps counting only adult men of Judah.
views.A: The Babylonian Chronicle (ABC 5, BM 21946) dates the fall of Jerusalem to 2 Adar of Nebuchadnezzar's 7th year. Ration tablets from Babylon list oil for "Ya'u-kinu king of Judah" and his five sons. The Lachish letters, from about 589–586, belong to the next crisis; Letter 3 mentions a commander, Coniah son of Elnathan, going down to Egypt. His father's name is the same as that of Jehoiachin's grandfather (24:8), which may or may not be the same family.
views.J: Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah or Coniah) was cursed by Jeremiah as childless (Jeremiah 22:30), yet he was the ancestor of Zerubbabel. Rabbinic tradition says he repented in prison and was forgiven, and that the curse was lifted (Leviticus Rabbah 19:6).
views.X: Matthew's genealogy names "Jechoniah and his brothers at the time of the deportation to Babylon" (Matthew 1:11–12), marking the exile as one of the three turning points of Israel's history leading to Christ.

deep.b: The Babylonian Chronicles are a series of tablets recording each year of a king's reign in a terse, mostly reliable style. The tablet for Nebuchadnezzar's first years (ABC 5, published by D. J. Wiseman in 1956) says that in his seventh year, in the month Kislev, he mustered his army, marched to Hatti, encamped against "the city of Judah," and on the second day of Adar took the city and seized its king. He appointed a king of his own heart and took its heavy tribute to Babylon. This is one of the most precisely dated events in the Old Testament: March 15/16, 597 BC. It agrees with 24:10–17 on the siege, the capture of the king, the new king and the plunder. Kings dates it to Nebuchadnezzar's eighth year (24:12); the difference probably comes from two ways of counting regnal years, or from the time it took to deport the captives in the spring of the new year.

Verse 2 names Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites and Ammonites. Many scholars suggest reading "Edom" for "Aram," since the two words differ in only one similar-looking letter (d and r) and Edom was hostile to Judah in this period (Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7); the Arad ostraca also speak of a threat from Edom. The suggestion is uncertain, and the Hebrew and the old translations have Aram.

echoes: Jeremiah 22:24–30; Jeremiah 24:1–10; Jeremiah 27:16–22; Jeremiah 52:28; 2 Chronicles 36:5–10; Ezekiel 1:1–3; Ezekiel 17:11–21; Daniel 1:1–2; Matthew 1:11–12

title: The Fall of Jerusalem
sum: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem for a year and a half. When famine has emptied the city of bread, the wall is breached; Zedekiah flees by night toward the Jordan, is caught near Jericho, and is brought to Riblah, where his sons are killed in front of him and his eyes are put out. A month later Nebuzaradan burns the temple, the palace and the great houses, breaks down the walls, carries off the bronze of the pillars, the Sea and the stands, and takes the people into exile. The chief priests and leaders are executed at Riblah. "And so Judah went into exile."

Babylon appoints Gedaliah, grandson of Shaphan, as governor at Mizpah. He urges the remaining commanders to serve Babylon, but Ishmael, of the royal line, assassinates him, and the survivors flee to Egypt. The book ends thirty-seven years after Jehoiachin's exile: the new king of Babylon releases him from prison, speaks kindly to him, sets his throne above the other kings and feeds him at his table every day of his life.
readings: Read as history

Archaeology in the City of David shows a thick layer of destruction from 586 BC, with burnt houses, arrowheads and bullae baked hard by the fire. Seals and bullae of officials named in these chapters have been found. The Babylonian ration tablets name Jehoiachin as a prisoner fed by the king.
Read as judgment fulfilled

Everything the prophets warned of comes to pass: the temple Solomon built is burned, the bronze he made is carried off, the line of David loses its throne, and the people go into exile, as Moses warned (Deuteronomy 28:36) and as Huldah said (22:16–17).
Read for the ending

Readers have long argued over the last four verses. Are they a closing note of hope for David's house, a bare report that the story is over, or a quiet sign that life in exile can be lived under the favor of a foreign king? See the deep section below.

views.H: A plain account of 588–586 BC, largely confirmed by Jeremiah 39–41 and 52 and by archaeology. The release of Jehoiachin in 561 is a real event, also reflected in the ration tablets of the years before it.
views.C: 25:1–21 is closely parallel to Jeremiah 52, which probably copied it. 25:22–26 is a short summary of Jeremiah 40–43. The last verses may have been added after 562 to an edition that once ended in 25:21 or 25:26; most date the final form to the exile.
views.A: The Lachish letters, written on potsherds as the Babylonians closed in (588–586 BC), speak of watching for the signal fires of Lachish because Azekah's could no longer be seen (compare Jeremiah 34:7). A seal reading "Jaazaniah servant of the king" was found at Tell en-Nasbeh, probably Mizpah. Babylonian ration tablets name Jehoiachin. The Al-Yahudu tablets record Judean exiles living in Babylonian villages a generation later.
views.J: The fast of the Ninth of Av marks the burning of the temple; the fast of Gedaliah (the third of Tishri) marks his murder (Bavli Rosh Hashanah 18b). Lamentations is read on the Ninth of Av. The rabbis reconciled the dates of 25:8 and Jeremiah 52:12 by saying the enemy entered the temple on the seventh, and the fire, set on the ninth, burned through the tenth (Bavli Taanit 29a).
views.X: Christian readers have seen in Jehoiachin's release a hint that God had not forgotten David's line, a hope Matthew traces to Jesus through Jehoiachin's grandson Zerubbabel (Matthew 1:12). Luke's list reaches Shealtiel and Zerubbabel through Neri instead (Luke 3:27), a well-known puzzle. The fall of Jerusalem became a lasting pattern for judgment in the New Testament (Luke 21:20–24).

deep.b: Between 1899 and 1917 German excavators at Babylon found about 300 tablets in a vaulted building near the Ishtar Gate. Ernst Weidner published four of them in 1939. Dated between Nebuchadnezzar's 10th and 35th years (595–570 BC), they record rations of oil and grain for foreign prisoners and workers at the palace, among them "Ya'u-kinu, king of the land of Yahudu," and "five sons of the king of Judah," with their attendant. This is Jehoiachin, still called king. The tablets show that Babylon treated him as a royal captive with a household, as 25:29–30 describes for his later years, and they confirm that he had sons, though Jeremiah 22:30 says none would sit on David's throne.

Kings could have ended with the temple in ashes or with the flight to Egypt. Instead it ends with a king in exile eating at a foreign table. Readers have heard this in three ways. A sign of hope. Gerhard von Rad and many others read it as a quiet signal that God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:16) still stands; H. W. Wolff saw in the book a call to the exiles to turn back to God, which leaves the same door open: the line survives, the king is honored, and the story is not over. Jewish and Christian readers who trace the Messiah through Jehoiachin's line read it this way. An epitaph. Martin Noth thought the Deuteronomistic History was a final verdict on Israel's failure, and that these verses only report the last fact known: the king lives on, but as a dependent. A way to live in exile. Others, among them Jon Levenson, see a lesson for exiles: Jehoiachin's fortune turns when he is under Babylon's favor, as Jeremiah urged the exiles to seek the welfare of the city where they lived (Jeremiah 29:7), and Israel's turning back to God might bring mercy (1 Kings 8:46–50). The words "lifted up the head" echo the cupbearer's dream that Joseph explained (Genesis 40:20), a release from prison that led to a greater rescue.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the book ends where it began
deep.b: The parallel between Jehoiachin at Babylon's table and Mephibosheth at David's (2 Samuel 9:7–13) is published: Jan Jaynes Granowski made it the center of her reading of the ending (1992), and it appears in several commentaries. Mephibosheth, the last of Saul's line, eats at David's table "always" (2 Samuel 9:13); now the last of David's line eats "always" at Babylon's, so that David's house receives the kind of mercy it once showed. What Claude adds is a wider frame: the books of Samuel and Kings open with a household eating at a sanctuary table in Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:4–9) and close with a king eating at a table not his own. If the frame is meant, the ending neither promises restoration nor rules it out, but places David's heir in the position of a guest who lives by a king's kindness. This frame is Claude's suggestion; the text makes no comment on its own last scene.

echoes: Jeremiah 39:1–10; Jeremiah 40:1–41:18; Jeremiah 52:1–34; 2 Chronicles 36:11–23; Lamentations 1–5; Psalm 137; Ezekiel 12:12–13; Ezekiel 33:21; Deuteronomy 28:36; Deuteronomy 28:68; Genesis 40:20; 2 Samuel 9:13; Matthew 1:11–12

settings.what: Gedaliah's oath to the commanders
settings.by: Gedaliah son of Ahikam, governor at Mizpah
settings.to: The commanders of Judah's scattered forces and their men
settings.when: After the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC
settings.why: 'Don't fear the Chaldeans' servants. Stay in the land. Serve the king of Babylon.' Gedaliah, of the family that protected Jeremiah, speaks the prophet's own advice (Jeremiah 27:11–12). His murder ends the hope of a settled life in the land, and the remnant flees to Egypt. For exiles it showed that rebellion against Babylon brought only more loss, and that waiting was the way left to them.
